projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert Mannheimer was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Could you tell us how you first got involved with the military way before the war started? How did that happen? And how did that -

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: I --I went to a school called Oregon State College. It's now a university. And I was enrolled in the ROTC Program. So I --because I thought I wanted to ride horses and they had a--the horses then, I was with them very serious. I opt for the last two years. However, as soon as I did that, they motorized the unit. So, but I did --I did ride horses my sophomore year. What the Army calls equitation.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: But you decided to --to stay on through the second two years?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah. So I --upon graduation --I graduated in 1939. And upon graduation I received a reserve commission -

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: --as the second lieutenant of field artillery.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Now, were you assigned to a reserve unit before the war began?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: I also went in the unit because I lived --I lived in Bend. Well --well --actually, I did --I was down here. But in Bend, there wasn't any unit except a National Guard Company. And that didn't take too many officers to fill it. So there wasn't any opportunity to do any reserve group training as long as you were in Bend. But I was down here before. I had a job here for a year before I went into the service.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Well, talk us through this decision to go on active duty that you made.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Well, I was working for an insurance agency. And I couldn't see any future in it. And I thought I better change occupations. I wasn't making any money. I think I got $75 a month or something like that and what I could pick up in commissions, which wasn't much. These were rough times. And so I decided to get my years of military service out of the way. Because we were told, those of us with reserve commissions would be required to spend a year active duty. They had just started the draft in September of '40. So another guy that worked for an insurance company and I decided one day that we join the Army. And we went over and signed up. And they sent us both out to Vancouver Barracks to take the physical. And he's the one that talked me into it, really. And he flunked the physical. So it ended up that I ended up in --in --about a month later I was --I got my orders for a year's active duty. And so I ended up in this Field Artillery Pack Unit at Fort Lewis.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Tell us a little bit about the 98th and 99th Pack Artillery. What was that like and what were the weapons and equipment like?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah. Well, the weapon was a Pack Howitzer. It's where it broke down into five parts and was carried -packed on five mules. And, of course, they had to have a special saddle, which was tailored to fit the conformation of the animal and --and the adaptor and so forth to hold everything. I can't remember. I know the tube was on one mule and the -I think the --(telephone ringing.) Oh, shoot.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. We were talking about the 98th Artillery Unit at Fort Lewis and you were talking about the mule loads, I think.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah. The maximum load was --for each mule was, I think, around pounds. But mostly around pounds per mule. They could carry quite a bit. And, again, they had to have separate mules to carry the ammunition and all of the hay and oats and everything. And in other words, and actually had four batteries in --this was a battalion. One of them was a --while they had three firing batteries, like normal artillery, one headquarters battery and one service battery. And the mules and the service battery were herded. And there is a strange story, a rare, funny story about that. We used to have a parade every, I guess, it was Saturday or something. And the word came down that every animal had to go on parade regardless of what. And the mules and service battery were herded. And they were wilder than the devil. There were about, I think they had a couple hundred of them. And they were the ones that they barely got to train for anything. So they would --everybody would pass and review. And then the service battery mob would come in there and the band would play and they'd all go wild. And they'd drag all the people all over the parade ground. It was a real mess. So I have an interesting story about that. I had a young West Point lieutenant who was my battery commander. And he called me in, I don't like the way our animals are performing in the parade. He says I want you to draw out --I think we had a drum and a --I don't know, a bugle and something else. And he says I want you to accustom our animals to music. And so I thought, you know, that was an order. So I got a detail man. We --every animal had a serial number burned in their neck so you can keep track of them. And by serial number we'd go through the group. And I'd tell them to blow the horn. And I don't --don't know what I was doing. About half way through when the battalion commander came along, of course, it was awfully hard to keep a straight face and tell him that I was accustoming the animals to music. And he told me I was doing it the wrong way. That besides the sound and whatnot, it was - it was the --it was the sight. And so, and so he said that you got to push the instrument up against their noses and do all this stuff. So they would lick the drum and everything. And we went through all that. Did it all over again. And then we had our next parade. And low and behold, the same thing happened. So I say that's why I stayed a second lieutenant so long.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: You and the mules?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: The mules and I didn't cooperate. But it was a lot of fun. It was --it was the nicest part of the --my service that I enjoyed. In other words, it was sort of like the country club. We had --we'd ride on Sunday. Everything was mandatory. You didn't say no. You know, it was the old Army. It was a regular Army unit. And we used to --we had an orderly. We didn't have to do any work. I had --I paid him five bucks extra and he kept the animals' hooves clean and curried and everything. I didn't have to do anything. Held my animal for me and shined my boots and whatever. And --and it was really like a country club. But we used to meet at the stable on Sunday and get --and get our animals. We were all assigned a horse, a regular, you know, just like they assign a Jeep or whatever. And then we'd jump logs and follow one another. Of course, all the second lieutenants were at the end of the line. And then meet back at the club and have a little --a few drinks and --and whatnot. So it was fun. I mean, I thought it was. I -I was having so much fun, I was ready to stay in the Army forever. However, I soon changed my mind after --after -after my months in Alaska.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, before we get to that, what kind of --can you talk about the uniforms and rifles and was that equipment modern stuff like the World War era or was that all left over from World War 1?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Well, none of us were familiar with World War 1. We had --in the 98th Pack, we had what was called a Pack Howitzer. And I think it was developed --they used a different one in the Spanish-American War. And I think they developed that in between. I don't know whether they ever used them in World War or not. But it was designed to fight in places that were inacceptable to the modern ways of getting around. In other words, trails and so forth, mountains, desert and things like that. Because a mule could walk down a trail and you couldn't get a Jeep down the trail. So that was the idea. It was a specialized unit. And I seemed to always get in specialized units or not like a division or anything like that. It was always something special seemed like.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: How about pre-war maneuvers? Anything like that happen up at Fort Lewis?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah. I --I signed up for one. In summer of '40, I thought, well, it was a way to get away from the job I didn't like. And so I signed up for this maneuver in which I understand that General Eisenhower, who was a lieutenant colonel at the time, was the maneuver director. Not that we ever met him or anything. But they assigned me to a field artillery battery, which was a portion of the National Guard. And we ran around the --oh, between Olympia and Fort Lewis. And --and it was interesting. And that was my first taste of what --of active duty. Two weeks. I got one way --well, that was before I got the point system, but it was one way of keeping active.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Now, do you go up to Alaska before Pearl Harbor or are you still at Fort Lewis when Pearl Harbor happened?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: No. I went there before Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Let's talk about how you wound up going to Fort Lewis ____.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: I was single. And that was my passport to Alaska and the --in one battery of field artillery out of this packet deal to Alaska, minus the mules. And so the fact that there were no accommodations for families at Kodiak, we were going to Kodiak only --in fact, I was transferred into the battery that went up there. I wasn't in it originally. Only the single guys like myself. There were four second lieutenants and a captain who was a regular Army West Point type of person. And that's -and we were sent to Kodiak. This was in, I think it --well, it was in September of '41, as protection for a Navy base that the Navy had an air station there. The Navy had most of the facilities at the time. I think one in Sitka and one in Kodiak and one at Dutch Harbor. And we were sent to Kodiak. One little battery of four Pack Howitzers, which didn't amount to much, but that's all the Army could spare. So I was there at the time of Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, let's talk a little bit about just kind of your first impression of the facility there in Kodiak and what things were like before the war started.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: That was sort of interesting. Because we went up there and we had never fired our artillery pieces. We picked them up at the dock in Seattle. We had never fired. When I say "we", the men had never fired their M rifles at which they were issued in lieu of carbines. They were supposed to get carbines in the artillery, but they hadn't manufactured them in any amount to give to the troops. So they were --we were issued M rifles. And so we went there, you know, kind of --it was kind of off the --and the strange part of it was, and it was kind of sad, I had a commanding officer who was a great guy, lots of fun. But as I said, he was more like a country club sort of a guy. He wasn't --he was not a --particularly a good commander. I liked him. But, we --for example, maybe I'm getting ahead of myself. But at the time of the Sunday morning that Pearl Harbor happened, we got the troops out. And we were trying to teach them, and we didn't know either, how to load and unload an M rifle. And we had the field manual in one hand and a blank bunch of --a cartridge with blanks in the other hand and going to every man showing them to load and unload an M rifle. And then everybody was issued, I think, live rounds of ammunition. And it was hardly worth your life to go around to check the guard. Because any twig that snapped, they'd probably let off a round of fire. I mean, everybody was edgy. Maybe I'm getting ahead of myself.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: No. That's fine. No. That's fine. So was this a pretty nice, permanent facility there or is this all pretty temporary?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: It was very temporary. As a matter of fact, the only nice part of it is, we did come up with nurses on the same boat. So we got to meet all the nurses. And there were, I think, of them. And so we had the edge on all the nurses there. And the strange part of it is that we -we got off of the ship and I remember seeing these wooden cantonment buildings. And I asked the jeep driver, I said where's ours? And he said wait 'til you see yours. So he takes us over to this place where they had the tents were in one end, not put up. They did have the floors down, the wooden floors. They were down in place, but you had to put your own tent up. And we lived like, you know, like it was a field operation. We had a tent mess hall, I think. But I think they cooked off of a field stove and mess kits. And it was that type of deal. On the other hand, the Navy, which ran everything, now, it's the same taxpayers, Navy place was deluxe. All those cantonments there were for the Navy. And they had --for example, they had a little club and they had a, I think they call it a mess steward, Black enlisted, mixing drinks all day. And they had a complete bathroom between every two rooms. They had --you had to share a bathroom with somebody else. But other than that, it was all complete. No latrines. No, you know, nothing in the field. And, of course, in their mess hall they ate on white table cloths with white napkins and all of the fancy things that the Navy does while we were out there in the field. So we found that out. So we'd run over there. And they had terrific food, steaks and everything we paid for. But I think that lasted about two weeks and then we were told that we weren't welcome anymore. The only --with two exceptions were, if we brought over one of our nurses, that was okay or if we were invited by a Naval officer. Otherwise, it was off limits; all their facilities. So that's --naturally, now, this is --this was during the peace-time part of it. And I don't recall whether --I don't think it changed any time I was there. But I figured, you know, we were all being subsidized by the same taxpayers. It doesn't seem particularly right, but the Navy ran Alaska. It was their --their deal, I found out. Now, the Army ran the Philippines when I was over there and the Navy were the second-class citizens. But as far as the --even though the Army had most troops up there, Navy didn't have very much up there. At Kodiak, for example, they --it was a --a Navel place. And they had a PBY --a few PBY's. That was it, maybe. I doubt if they had people in the whole -the whole thing, but we --we had quite a few troops.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: How were --were the guns in position ready to fire, or what was that like or __________+++++.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Well, after Pearl Harbor, my commanding officer decided that we found a place, they had to practically build a road into where we could cover several of the possible landing places. In other words, this Howitzer had a maximum range of, as I remember, around 9,000 yards, which is a little less than two miles. And they were accurate little pieces, but they were 75's. They were very low power as things went. And we had four of them. And we built shelters out of the dunnage because it rained a lot up there. And we manned them on a 24-hour basis, changing the crew all the time. We were on alert. Now, the strange --an interesting deal I keep thinking about, the night before the morning of Pearl Harbor day, I --this commanding officer that I had was kind of bitter because he was the only one of us that was married that was up there. And so he found a loophole in the regulations to bring his family up there. He had a wife and one little boy. So he --he had the same trouble, I guess I do, talk too much. He told an infantry colonel about what it was like. So it ends up when the boat came up there, I think it was a day before Pearl Harbor, a day or two before, who was on the boat was the colonel's family, not his. So he proceeded to take it pretty bad. In fact, he got lousy drunk the night before. And he was going to retire from the Army. He was --I shared a tent with him. So I got to know him pretty well. And we were in the --and, of course, the next morning about 7:30 the charge of quarters came around, told him to report to the general. We had a one-star general there, General Corlett. And about an hour later, he came back. I was still in the sack. And he said get out, we're at war. And that's how I found out about Pearl Harbor. And again, that's where we went through the rigamarole of trying to instruct the men on how to load and unload an M rifle, which is kind of sad. Plus, the other thing that I --I had been to Fort Sill. And I was the only one that had recently been to Fort Sill. Well, one of the --one of the guys had been there, but he had equitation. Of course, he didn't have the gunnery course. And I went through the gunnery course mainly because of I was the worst shot of anybody in the battalion. So they decided to send me there to learn how to --what it was all about. It helped a lot. But, actually, what happened was that I decided that we should adjust, you know, adjust the guns, because we never fired them. We wanted to fire the darn things. And --and so I got a --managed to get a survey from the contractors that were there that were going to make a long-base intersection and fire out to sea. It was the only place we could do it. Of course, we'd had to warn everybody to stay away. And everything was all set to go ahead and do it until I made a request for ammunition. And I think I asked for five rounds per Howitzer and four Howitzers. That's rounds, something like that, to get an average, so forth. And the request was denied because there were only, I think, rounds on the island. And that piece that we had was capable of, in a fire fight of firing five rounds a minute. So you figure we wouldn't have lasted very long if we did get attacked. And it was kind of a sad way to --you figure as long as I was there, never fired any of the --of the - However, I didn't stay there. Because I had -there was another fella and I who had graduated in the same ROTC. In fact, two other guys that graduated in my same ROTC class. That one of them went on duty on the same orders that I did. So we were of equal rank. And so he was after Pearl Harbor happened. The captain went to headquarters. The general decided to get him in on headquarters. So we were left with four second lieutenants. And he was the battery commander. We got along all right. But they decided -they had a call for --to send one second lieutenant to Anchorage, which was where the 81st was. And it was a complete battalion. And first they asked for volunteers and none of us wanted to go. Although, I ended up going. And I got the best, I think, of the deal, but I didn't know it at the time. And so they had drew for --with straws. And this other guy drew the short straw right off the bat, but he was in love with a nurse. And he also had a friend in the --who was the general's aid. So they ended up sending me against my will. I mean, I didn't have any choice. I was told to go. But it was the best thing that happened, I think, because they got lost down --down the chain. I can see I'm not interesting him very much. TAPE OPERATOR: No. I'm listening. I'm just trying to change the tape.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Are we about done?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: No. We're not even close, sir. You're not close to done. TAPE OPERATOR: No. Just checking the tape here.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Okay. All right. Yeah. Well, anyway, I ended up in Anchorage. And Anchorage is the banana belt, as Alaska went. In other words, they had about 10,000 people there. There was a --the post was practically next to town. There was Elmendorf Field right there. And it had all the facilities that a lot of us at Kodiak didn't have. And as that unit went down the chain, I think they went to Adak or somewhere afterwards, they were kind of lost, just one little battery. So I think it was in February of '42 I went to Anchorage. And I stayed with that unit until, I guess it was July '44. I was in there for a long period of time.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So you were at Anchorage then when the Japanese invaded the Aleutian chain and bombed Dutch Harbor? What was that like?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Right. Right. Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What was that like?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Well, that was interesting. Because then that's the reason, I guess, that --well, one of the reasons we ended up in Nome. I was in Anchorage. And they bombed Dutch Harbor and landed on Kiska and that, too. And so we --they were pretty well prepared. They had, I guess they call --gosh, I've forgotten what they call them, but they had this place that they had all set up for to go and in case of they were attacked. And they'd --I saw the unit made kind of a cave into a hill all along. And they put wooden bunks in. So we were pretty well prepared. And that's where we went, right. And we were there for a week or two. Unfortunately, everybody got yellow fever, jaundice because of the -

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Let's change tapes one more time.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Of all things, they decided to inoculate all the troops up there with yellow fever serum. Here we're in Alaska, there wasn't any way of getting it and it was an imperfect serum. And everyone got yellow jaundice. In fact, a sad story I remember. On the day that we left for --the day before we left --we flew into --flew to Nome, half the battery was in Nome and half of it --I was on the last part of it to go up there. And we had a poor guy who had --was real sick. And so I sent him to the --the doctor. And they said he's got to go to the hospital. I sent him to the hospital. And they sent him back because we didn't have a sick book. It was up in Nome. Now, this is the way the Army operated. And -and he came back. And I called him up and told him, I said, you know, what are we going to do, the guy is sick. I sent him up again. They still sent him back because we didn't have a sick book. Finally, we got him in the hospital. Then we were found after he got to Nome that he died, which was stupid. But that's the way things happened in the Army. But it got so that I got a slight case of it. But a lot of people, you couldn't tell where the pupils in the rest of the eye, where they were because they got --it got so yellow, dark and whatnot. It was wicked. And it was all unnecessary because it was through this serum that he had for yellow fever. So that was one of the nasty things that happened. And the thing about --say we went out --we were all there for about a week or two. Another interesting thing, just before we went to Nome, they had an island out in Cook Inlet. If you're familiar with how you get into Anchorage, there's a --Cook Inlet is the waterway in there. And there was an island about four or five miles out there. And so we had a field artillery piece on the island. We were supposed to --if you were out there, the ships that came in, we were supposed to intercept them, see if they're friendly or something else. How you could do anything with a little, they call them J boats, they were like oversize rowboats. And, I mean, they can run over you like - The main thing was, as soon as the ship came in there, we'd radio back and get a clearance. Because if you had to try to board it, it was practically impossible. But I was out there for a week. And in they sent --they sent me to carrier pigeon school because they were training carrier pigeons. So they'd bring out a fresh bunch of carrier pigeons. And then every day or so we'd write a little note, put it in there, they had a little capsule on their leg, and launch it. And they were supposed to go back home. I don't know whether they did or not, but that was part of training. So you see, we had a lot of different experiences. I had several others that were kind of odd, too.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Like what?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Well, one thing at Nome, because it was isolated, we didn't --they didn't --they made a --they had a special general court there. And because we had a lot of --being in Nome was more of a nut problem than anything else. These guys went nuts about the isolation, whatnot. It was very isolated. They had a lot of trouble with their --you know, we didn't have any action, but we had a lot of problems, mental problems. And they found out that if they got three special court martial's, that they figured that then they'd --that was one way of getting out of Alaska. They could send them to Leavenworth and rehabilitate them and whatnot, or at least that was what the guardhouse deals. I'm not a lawyer. Never been a lawyer. But I was made the trial judge advocate of a general court and which is sort of unique. In fact, I was very seriously thinking about going to law school when I got out. And I applied at Eugene at the University of Oregon and they said they would let me in but I'd have to wait. While I waited, I went to work and decided I'd never get to law school, I guess. But --but it was sort of interesting. I mean, trying these cases and taking depositions and being -acting like a Perry Mason and so forth. But that was one odd experience. And, you know, in the Army, when you get the order, you do anything, as you well know.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, I heard that the war was a big boon to Alaska, that the number of people in Alaska went way up, there was a lot of stuff up there during that time. You were there during that time _______++++. Talking over each other.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: I think --I think that happened after the war, as I remember. One thing I do remember, sort of interesting. Again, I spent months in Nome. And that's the end of everywhere at that time. There wasn't a lot there. But there was a guy there that --that had the dock. And he got so much a ton for everything that was brought in. So he was making a fortune. And, but he just happened to be at the right place at the right, you know, the right time. Plus the fact that you couldn't live in a tent because of the weather. So they had to bring in Quonset huts. And you couldn't --and Nome is an ice-bound port so you couldn't bring in --you know, you had to bring in food and everything, all everything before the port froze up. So it was --there was quite a lot of activity. In fact, at one time, I think we had about, I don't know, I can't remember, or ships out there waiting to get unloaded. A lot of them. And it didn't have a dock. They had --they had to anchor a couple miles off shore and lighter everything in. And this guy had the --he had the --they had a little river there where they had a dock where the lighters could come in. And they had, we call them, well, Eskimos, or Klutes or whatnot. They were -mostly did the thing. One of the things that --I probably shouldn't say this, but one of the things that I --I had discussed with the Merchant Marine were that they were up there on these ships sitting on their butt and we had to put the men up there to unload the things down in the hole, run the winches through everything. That wasn't in their contract, but they were up there drawing down disaster pay for being --and --and our men were doing all of the work. Because I had to --I got duty on the ship. Of course, the ship's crew couldn't order any men, our men to do anything. They had to have an officer there to give the order. They would tell us what they wanted, then you would tell the men what you wanted. So I got that duty 'cuz I found out that they had fresh food and everything and we didn't have that. We were living on reindeer meat. If you have every eaten reindeer, that was the only meat other than Spam and Vienna Sausage, all that junk. I mean, that reindeer meat was like goat. It was real wild. I mean, because they were just eating tundra berries and whatnot. They didn't have anything decent to eat. The natives up there had herds of reindeer just like we had cattle down here. They were --and so they bought the meat from the natives, brought it in. Wasn't very good. So I got up there for a few days. Then they had all this confusion on the dock and they made me go back to the dock to get things straightened out. So I didn't get to stay there very long. But I was working on the dock one night. I had the crew. We were getting everything off and sent out to the different places to be stored. They had these Butler huts they stored them in. They called them -they were made by Butler, I guess. And this fella that owned the dock came around to me and he said, looked down, he says, how long have you been in the Army? You're --he said you're still a second lieutenant. I said yes, sir. He said how long have you been in the Army? I said I think it was --I said months. He says you're still a second lieutenant? I said yes, sir. He said well, there is something wrong because my son just graduated from OCS at Fort Sill a month ago and he got his promotion to first lieutenant. You should be having the promotion up here instead of him. But I said that would be fine, but doesn't work that way. Because again, it was a tight deal once you got up there. This general we had, his name was --what the heck was it? I can't think of his name right now. He got killed in Okinawa. He was fighting with McArthur, I found out, who was going to make the push to --whether it was the northern route or the southern route. And once he got there, he wouldn't let any troops go until they wiped -they cleaned Kiska and that out, too. Then we were, as a unit we were recycled back to the States. So anyway, this fellow on the dock got ahold of me and he said, about oh, an hour or so later, he motioned to me, said come in here, I want to give you something. So I went in a warehouse or something. He reached in a gunny sack and he pulls out a fifth of scotch. And he said maybe this will make you feel better. So I said, well, I don't know whether I should take it. I want you to have it anyway. I took it back to my --I was living in a tent with the battalion chaplain. We were sharing a tent. He was a Catholic priest. Heck of a good guy. And so I showed him this bottle and I said look what I got on the dock. And I put it in my --I don't know, a foot locker or something. Then I --I think I showed it to him a couple other times. I didn't really like scotch very well. And one day I was looking at him. And I was kind of --I didn't understand Catholic priests, I guess. I was looking at him. I could see that he was pretty much interested in my bottle. So I asked him, I said, do you want to join me for a drink? And he says I thought you'd never ask. And we killed this bottle of scotch that night. So, anyway, it --we didn't get promoted up there. I did get promoted really after that. I finally got a promotion to first lieutenant. But I was a second lieutenant, I think, for, like, months. And that was on active duty. And I know --I remember we had --there was a general called --he built --he was in charge of building the ALCAN Highway. Gosh, I can't --Hoag. His name was Hoag. And his son was in our unit. He was a nice guy. But his son had graduated from West Point after I'd been in the Army a year. And he was a second lieutenant until his dad showed up there. The next day he got promoted to first lieutenant. So I knew where I stood. But those are just reflections, I mean, and I did finally get a promotion.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Ever have any run-ins with the wildlife up in Alaska?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Not personally. I saw a Kodiak bear stuffed. One of the things that was interesting, we had a, I think it was Alabama National Guard Unit at Kodiak with us. And so they decided to go out and hunt bear once. And they killed a Kodiak bear, but they didn't have a license. And at the time, it cost $50 in Alaska. And Alaska was a territory. So it was through the U.S. Commissioner you got a license. So they --they confiscated the carcass, of course. And then he made a deal with them if he will get it stuffed and send it back to his university back in Alabama, wherever it was, if he could --he could keep it. They let him do it. They had to buy the license, I think, maybe pay a fine or something. I don't know. But I never --we were instructed in Kodiak never to go out without arms because of these Kodiak bear. They're huge, you know. But other than that, lots of fish. Lots of salmon. And, of course, the --around Nome, we called them Klutes, native ladies' would --would --after they'd cut, they'd notch the salmon and put it out and let it dry so it was just brittle and hard and they fed the dogs that, the sled dogs and whatnot. There was a lot of - As a matter of fact, we had --one of the funny things, there was a priest that had a colony on what's called King Island, which was just out a short distance off the mainland at Nome. And he got sick and couldn't get out there this one winter because the ice came and couldn't -froze up. So he had to stay in Nome. So he would come out to --with my former roommate --my --he got a better --this chaplain that I was talking about got transferred to the Air Corp. He got a better deal with the Air Corp. So he was there with the Air Corp. And he and this priest came, would come to -we'd have these parties. And they'd come up in a dogsled. I can still see 'em racing up there and my former roommate holding onto dear life while they were coming up there. Another thing that's interesting, at Nome we had --I'm wandering a lot, we had --that was one stop for the Russian Land Lease Program. And they --they flew the planes to Fairbanks with White Stars and then they painted them red in Fairbanks and we got a Russian crew to take 'em over. And the first stop was Nome. Then the next stop was Siberia. Isn't very far. I think it was about miles where they --they had this base. Nobody knew much about it or anything. But they built a big, long strip out of tailings from the --Nome, you know, had been a gold rush deal. They had all --they had two or three dredges still working there mining gold and they had all these tailings from and they built an airstrip out of, a big, long airstrip. So the Russians brought their --their stuff in there. And they had a Russian colonel and a Russian major that were stationed there with a Russian ground crew. So we had an officer in our outfit who was Polish. And he could talk enough similar language to Russian that he became the general's aid in charge of taking care of the Russians. So, again, this was a regular Army unit, the 81st Field Artillery. And my --we had --we called them the gold dust twins. I shouldn't call them that, I guess. But they were two regular army officers that ran the thing. And one was the battalion commander and one was the exec. And they wanted to make points with the Russians so they asked Crolicki (ph), who was our Polish guy, to bring the Russians up for dinner one night. And I was in headquarters battery, so it was our mess. And they had this Russian colonel was in --he never cracked a smile. It was all business. And he didn't talk any English that --except he probably knew a lot more than we knew, but he would never talk any English or anything else. Then they had the executive officer, who was a major. He was the PR guy. He'd slap you on the back and tell jokes and, you know, a regular guy and whatnot. And he was kind of fun to be around. Well, we had both of them there. I remember we were trading, showing pictures of our girlfriends and wives and whatnot. And these Russians could drink a lot. They would take --they didn't bother about chaser or anything else. They would take a glass of booze and go like that, have more. They'd get kind of loaded, but didn't matter. They liked to drink. And anyway, we were showing off these pictures. And I'll always remember this major got out his billfold. And he had a whole bunch of ladies' pictures. And he had a kind of an older woman. He pointed to that. He said mother. And he talked kind of pigeon English. And then he had another --another one. He pointed to that. He said sister. Seester. (ph) Oh, yeah, fine. We go back -anyway, finally, got to the sweater girl and he said girlfriend. So regardless of what country you're in, everybody has got the same idea, what Army you're in or what Air Force you're in. So sort of interesting. But, you know, the Russians were up there. And it was kind of different.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: A lot of --a lot of planes flying through there headed for Russia?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Sometimes when the weather was good they'd get or so backed up before they could go across. And the other thing that was interesting, they used --they made maximum use of their pilots. They would come in there with bandages on their head. They had been wounded or something. But if they could still fly a plane, they were flying the ferrying route to bring in all these land-leased planes, you know. And I understand --I didn't fly with them, but everybody said once you flew with them they were --they would scare the hell out of them.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: That's what I understood. (Talking over each other.)

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah. Okay. They --they didn't --they didn't --they weren't too careful about. The other thing we were talking about, the 10th Mountain Division. When I was at Nome, an order came down for us to furnish a cadre to go to Camp Hale for the 10th Mountain Division. And I think there was, like, men. And --and since I was the only officer that had pack artillery experience, they put me on the cadre. In fact, I picked the cadre. And what I was trying to --in the Army, when something like that comes down, they --everybody tries to unload all their --their baggage on. And so I tried to get halfway decent people. It wasn't always possible, but, I mean, as much as you could. I was --pretty much having been in the battalion a while, I was --pretty well knew what to pick. So we get to Anchorage. Then I find out that they didn't want an officer. So they sent me back to Nome, which was --I --but the men went out and they went to Camp Hale. And I'm sure that was the cadre for the 10th Mountain Division. We didn't know that. The they were -the orders were to go to Camp Hale. And, of course, to get out of Alaska was -everybody looking forward to it. In fact, I had I don't know how many things that --giving me deals to call their wives and call there this and that to tell them all about whatever it was. Do me a favor and call so and so. And I never got there. So, however, we did --after they cleaned up Kiska and that too, they --first of all, we went to Dutch Harbor. I spent six months at Dutch Harbor.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What was that like?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Well, that was a lot better than Nome in a lot of ways because it was a fresh water or an ice-free port. And we got --got good food. We got everything that we -a lot of things we had missed up in Nome. Plus the fact they had a sub base there and a lot of men got problems with torpedo juice. I know I was a battery commander by that time. And I had a couple run-ins with submarine people and their torpedo juice. And as you know, that was a common practice in the Navy. And that was a big --ended up it was a pretty good size Navel base. Much larger than what was at Kodiak at the time we were there. And we were scheduled to go to AD (ph). And then they cleaned up the --chased the Japanese out of --well, Kiska was the last deal. They left before they got there. And then they had --they had a fire fight after that, too. But they didn't use us. They didn't use anybody that had been up there any time. They brought in a division that had been trained for desert warfare on the desert and put them --sent them to AD (ph). And they weren't equipped. They had gangrene. They didn't have the right shoes or didn't have anything. And they demoted the general in the field of battle to colonel, I think. And he was reprimanded, but I don't know if all of that was his fault. They shouldn't have sent those kind of people up there in the first place, but that's the stupidity of the Army. And they paid the price. They lost quite a few people to that, too. A lot of them through weather. I read an interesting book called Thousand War --Thousand Mile War. I don't know whether you -

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: It's a good book.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: And it documented a lot of things that I didn't know about at the time, I found out about. Like the fact that General Buckner was his name, was trying to v-i-e (ph) with McArthur for the northern route to go to --from the Aleutians to jump in the, I think there was a Kuril Isles and there was other Japanese islands up there. And that's one of the reasons why they wouldn't let any of us out of there. And I think all of the time, I know it's kind of a rough deal in Iraq and whatnot, but these are guys on a, what, a six month deal and they rotate, whatnot. With us, once you were in there, you never got out. It was a different --a different type of situation. So, but, I found out quite a bit about --after reading that book. It was an interesting book. I --we didn't know at the time. We were just up there, you know.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So Dutch Harbor, I guess you were just there again to protect the base and -

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Well, actually we got re-equipped there. The 81st was in an interesting --it was another made-to-order outfit. They had two batteries of French 75's, the old World War 75, but they were modified with a split trail. And they had one battery of GPF's World War guns. Again, a French gun. And the idea was they were both coast artillery and field artillery. The one battery was supposed to be coast artillery. So then after about the time I got to the 81st they had a cold weather testing station up in Fairbanks. And they had, I think it was a Pack Howitzer and a Howitzer up there to cold test it. And they sent it down to --and it became part of this one Battery C, which was the ones that had the GPS. So they had kind of a provisional deal on the side. So it was a real bastard outfit. So they sent us to Dutch Harbor and issued us Howitzers. And we're supposed to go to AD (ph) with Howitzers. However, after everything was cleaned up we went --they sent the unit to Camp Chaffee, Arkansas, and became Howitzers, not the World War version, but the World War version. And they went to Europe, but I didn't go with them. And which is kind of a sad deal, but I didn't get along with the commanding officer. I was always in trouble. And I didn't get along. I don't --sometimes I wonder why I even stayed in the Reserves because --but I had a lot fun in the Reserves. It wasn't always that fun. But I didn't get a long with the commanding officer so he decided to send me back to Fort Sill for further training. That was his excuse. He wouldn't tell me, except I knew we --we had some differences. And they went to Europe. And they were with Patton and part of --on the fringe of the Battle of the Bulge. And I went --I ended up going to the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: He might have done you big a favor.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah, probably did. I had a lot of big favors by accident, I mean -

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, what do you think of the, you know -

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: --when I went to the commanding general staff school is right when they had the ______ to --back in, like, right around 1990, right in there.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah. Well, that's -

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: And the unit I was being assigned to went away. So they kept me at Leavenworth and I taught there three years.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Well, you got a lot more out of it than I did. We were just --we were only back there for two weeks, but you understand it's a five-year course.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: I understand that.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: It was interesting. It was the most interesting part of my Army training that I ever had, I think.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: It was --it's a good school. Anyway, tell me, when you transitioned to the 105's, did you think that was a pretty good weapon? What did you think?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Well, they are a lot better than the 75's. They had a lot of the advantages. Besides more fire power, they had --the was a fixed deal and it was a flat-trajectory weapon. And it --again, it had a split trail, but it was limited and in the amount of elevation you could get. So you couldn't fire on the back of a hill or anything like that, which you could with a Howitzer where they went up the elevation, go on the backside, and what do they call them, deflate or whatever. And they had a lot of advantages, though. It was --well, it was the standard support artillery piece of World War 2. And I think they still use them.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Yeah. They do. Actually, is part of their main artillery.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah. It was copied from the Germans, more or less in a lot of the features and -

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: And then you moved on to the 155, which was the biggest gun, pretty much, at the time. So what was that like?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Well, no, I was an eight-inch Howitzer, which was when I went to the Philippines and before. And they were a terrific weapon. They were big, but they were very accurate. I mean, the probability error was practically nil. You could fire in the same hole practically for -and, I don't know, are we still talking or -

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Uh-hum.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Anyway, you know, what happened was that they were --we were sent to the --well, you know what it was all about. We were sent to the Philippines. And that was a staging area to land on the island of Japan. And lots of people were --I mean, it was --it was --they had an awful lot of troops there. And I remember my brother was in a --was in the 86th Infantry Division. And he was in Europe for, I don't know, he was in a couple fire fights. I think he was there for maybe three or four months. And then VE-day happened and they transferred the unit to the Pacific for the landing on Japan. And they were halfway across the Pacific when J-day happened. They didn't turn around. He ended up there. In fact, I got a note I was --one night that, that he was about miles away. So I went over and found him. So I saw quite a bit of him. But I didn't stay in the Philippines long after that. I had enough points. But being in Alaska, that I got out fairly --fairly soon, but -

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, take me from Fort Sill, the Advanced Course.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: You must have gone to another unit and then prepared and deployed.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah. After I graduated from the Advanced Course at Sill, I got into the ____+ Unit. What they did was, what the Army did, they took a number of coast artillery units that they had, particularly on the East Coast and that were fixed units and transferred them into heavy artillery pieces, which they figured were more useful to --and this one that I was in was one of those. It was a National Guard Unit. The commanding officer was a National Guard officer. A great guy. He was real good to me. Treated me much nicer than the regular Army people did, as far as I was concerned, and in a lot of respects. I know I --as a sidelight, my father was dying. And we were stationed at a place called Fort Leonardwood, Missouri. He was in Chicago and expected to die any time. And it was Thanksgiving, about this time of the year. And so I guess I looked pretty depressed. And he asked me what was the matter and I told him. And he said I just lost my father. He said, why don't you take the weekend off and I'll give you basket leave, you know, BO/CO basket leave. Was a heck of a nice thing to do. He said we'll keep the thing in the basket to protect you. And so I took off. And I had Thursday, Friday and Saturday and came back Sunday night and went to Chicago. And my dad died about two weeks later. So he was --and, in fact, I visited him. He retired to Fort Myers, Florida, and I had a chance to visit with him one time. Then --in fact, then he died and we spent the night with his widow, my wife and I.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Now, you --you were in Artillery through the whole war?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Although, you weren't in --necessarily in combat, but you were given a lot of instruction, had the experience?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: A lot of people say that, that the American Artillery was probably the best of anybody's in the war. Can you put a finger on why that might be or what could have made the difference?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Well, they came a long ways. Now, when I joined the 81st Field Artillery, they had --their officers hadn't been to the latest version of Fort Sill where they taught massing a whole battalion on one by a - And they also --they issued us --in fact, we had a wooden version, or a paper version of --it was a logarithmic slide rule in which you could figure data on very fast. They were still doing it in the 81st when I got there the old-fashioned way where they had the S3 gunnery officer and had a sergeant there. And they were doing it longhand, so to speak. And it took 'em forever to get the data out. And so you tried to tell them what you were doing. You didn't dare because this is a regular Army unit and we don't need any advice from any of you young so and sos out of Fort Sill. As you know how that probably goes. So that was one thing. And they could mass a whole division. They learned about tieing it in and on -on a target, if necessary. But battalion, a division, the old World War days and the lot, the pre-war American Army were operating as batteries. And in other words, everybody went up and did their own little thing by battery. And, you know, and I think that was the --one of the things. Plus, the equipment got a lot better. They finally got around to get some --I --I'm not too --I've been retired long enough, so I don't know what they're doing now, but -

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: It's --they got computers now.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Yeah, I know. Well, we had a --my unit in the 81st had a reunion at Fort Carson. I guess this is four or five years ago. Colorado Springs is where we had the reunion. And then we went out to Fort Carson and we toured an outfit. And we went in the mobile deal where all the computers were and whatnot. I didn't know exactly what it was all about, but at least I got a taste of what they're doing now.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Would have been a self-propelled artillery battery fired direction sitting on tracks and stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: I don't recall whether it was a self-propelled or told. But, anyway, still use the same, you know, fire direction equipment as all on the computer and -

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Pretty high speed. Well, what do think your time in the service did for you then, either did for you or to you?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: Well, I'd say this, that I went in the service and I was only, like, or years old. And I was a pretty green sort of a person. I --you know. And I think in all due respect, I had some hard knocks and some good knocks. And I think it helped shape --my --my life, so to speak. And I --I think I was more, much more mature. Of course, I was in for five and a half years, so I had a lot of time to season or, so to speak. But I don't think it did me any harm. I was lucky in a lot of ways. Because I was lucky in everywhere I went. I didn't think so always, but I was lucky in that I didn't --I wasn't in any particular danger.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Well, is --is there just anything else, Bob, that you'd like to say?

sp.speaker: Robert Mannheimer
sp.p: I don't know. I think I've pretty well covered the field, I --I think. So sometimes when --during the five and a half years, you know, I felt like I wish I wasn't there, but I think all in all I think about it, it was probably the things that I think about and talk more about in my life than --because other than that, I haven't had a very exciting life. It's been more drab. Trying to make a living and raise a family and the usual things. And I --I don't know. I wonder at the time -at the time I got very disillusioned with the Army at the end. And I don't --I know I went through a separation center. And they asked me if I wanted to stay in the Reserve. And I said, well, I don't really care whether I do or not. So that was enough to say yes. Although, I didn't come out and beg. And that was the smartest thing that I did by accident sort of. Because, as you know, it's --I'm enjoying a terrific deal. I get paid every month. I get Tri Care with both my medicine and my medical. And the Army really has treated me pretty well, or the taxpayers have, I should say. And I'm lucky. Because at my age, we need all those things. That's about all I can say.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: All right.
